description:
Mars is closer than you think
We're six crewmates from Jordan on a classified mission: prove that Mars isn't 225 million km away, it's been hiding in plain sight right here on Earth. Armed with NASA data, dangerous amounts of coffee, and a strict "Code, Debug, Repeat" lifestyle, we're hunting down every place on our planet that looks sus-piciously Martian.
summary:
Before astronauts walk on the Moon or Mars, they rehearse on Earth, as NASA did in Arizona in 2024 for the first crewed Artemis landing. Yet, as this challenge notes, such analog sites are not well characterized.

Mars Among Us is a web tool that finds and ranks Earth's twins of the Moon and Mars, using NASA data. Compare ranks 30 Earth analog sites for any of NASA's nine Artemis regions or a Mars site and a mission, factor by factor, with a source for every number; missing values are left out, never guessed. Discover compares all 86,498 land patches on Earth with a known analog. Given no landform data, it led from Canada's Tuktoyaktuk pingos to Alaska, where 1,247 pingos are mapped, and from Death Valley to coastal Peru, where dust devil tracks are mapped. Known analogs rank in its top 0.8% of land (random: 2.5%). Closest to Mars ranks all ice-free land against Mars itself; Earth's most Mars-like land is western Tibet. Never given a list of analogs, it puts Licancabur, used by NASA's High Lakes Project, in the top 0.24% of Earth's land and Tso Kar, where India's space agency ran its HOPE mission, in the top 0.41%.

We state where the analogy stops: no place on Earth has the Moon's vacuum or Mars's radiation.

It helps mission planners choose where to rehearse, researchers find new candidate regions, and students see how Earth relates to the Moon and Mars, with every number sourced.
details:
What it does

Mars Among Us answers one question: where on Earth is the twin of a given place on the Moon or Mars, for a given job? The twin depends on the job and on the region: for Malapert Massif on the Moon, the best Earth site to test a rover is Lofoten, Norway (100%, on 3 of 4 factors), but the best to prepare a permanent base is Taylor Valley, Antarctica (75%, 4 of 5); for the crater-rim regions such as Haworth and Nobile Rim, it is Haughton Crater, Canada (80%, all 5 factors).

Why it matters

Before astronauts walk on the Moon or Mars, they rehearse on Earth: NASA’s JETT5 test in May 2024 sent crews on simulated moonwalks in Arizona to prepare the first crewed Artemis landing. As this challenge notes, such analog sites are not well characterized, and choosing one means reading scattered papers by hand. Mars Among Us puts that search in one place, with the evidence for every number, and extends it to all of Earth’s land.

How it works

  • Compare. Each mission compares its own factors (slope, rock type, landform, mean temperature, day–night swing, aridity, ice, frozen ground, ground ice). Each factor scores strong (100%), partial (50%) or weak (0%) after the NASA-led analog framework of Stern et al. (2025, JGR Planets); the match is the average of the factors that have a published value. Missing values are left out, never guessed, and the page shows how many factors a score is based on. Moon targets are measured from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA sunlight and shadow, Diviner temperature and stable ice, Mini-RF radar) within 7.5 km of each region’s centre; Mars slope comes from MOLA; Earth slope and elevation from ASTER GDEM; Earth ground temperature from MODIS. Orbital images of both places are shown side by side at the same scale.
  • Discover. Every 0.5° land cell (86,498 in all) is compared with a known analog on seven traits: mean temperature, day–night swing, precipitation and wind (NASA POWER, 2001–2020), mean elevation and relief (SRTM-based terrain tiles), and rock class (GLiM). Each trait scores 100% when equal and falls linearly to 0% at a stated gap; the match is the mean. The page shows, for each trait, how far apart the two places are, the country of each result, and why the starting site stands in for the Moon or Mars, with its source.
  • Closest to Mars. Mars is colder and drier than anywhere on Earth, with thinner air and a bigger day–night swing, so no Earth value can equal Mars’s. Each of the 61,443 ice-free land patches is ranked on each condition: its percentile is the share of ice-free land it is more Mars-like than (colder, drier, higher so thinner air, bigger swing). The index is the mean of the four, 0–100. Mars values are from NASA’s Mars Fact Sheet; Earth values from NASA POWER and SRTM-based terrain. Ice sheets are left out: Mars’s surface is rock and dust.
  • Earth Analogs. 24 known analog sites on a map, grouped by the 15 Mars landform classes of DoMars16k plus the Moon, each with its published research and the geomorphic process behind it.

How to use the site

The site has six pages, reached from the top menu on a computer or the tab bar at the bottom of a phone. Every page opens with the same three numbered steps, and every view has its own link, so a result can be shared exactly as seen.

  • Home. The idea in one minute: what an analog is, how the site works in three steps, and who it helps. Below that are the new twins Discover found, each marked Confirmed (with the published study) or Lead (not yet studied), with a “See it on the map” button; Earth’s most Mars-like land with the agencies’ sites that rank near it (“See the ranking”); and a worked example from Compare.
  • Compare (where should we train?). 1) Choose a place: one of NASA’s nine Artemis landing regions near the Moon’s south pole, or a site on Mars such as Jezero Crater. 2) Choose the job: rover testing, a base, a permanent Moon base, local resources, search for life or astronaut training. 3) The answer comes first: the best place on Earth and its percentage. “See why” opens the explanation: each factor as strong, partial or weak, the sum that gives the percentage, and “Show the evidence” with the value on both sides and its source. Orbital images of the target and the Earth site are shown at the same scale. The list below ranks the top Earth sites (“Show all 30 Earth sites” for the rest); clicking one shows its explanation. Further down, “What we know about” the target gives its LRO measurements: sunlight, permanent shadow, temperature, stable ice and radar.
  • Discover (where else on Earth?). 1) Pick a start site, a place already used to study the Moon or Mars; the page says why it stands in for the Moon or Mars, with its source. 2) Optionally narrow the search: “Only look at” a rock type (volcanic, sedimentary, metamorphic) or a climate (desert, hyper-arid, cold, or ESA permafrost). 3) The map colours every patch at least 60% alike, from light orange to bright yellow; a legend explains the colours and markers. The list shows the 10 closest regions, at least 400 km apart, each with its country and whether it is already a known analog. Opening one shows a table of the seven traits for both places, the sum behind the match, where the analogy breaks down, and NASA’s ASTER terrain relief inside the patch on the map. The map’s layer button switches between satellite, OpenStreetMap and MODIS ground temperature for January and July.
  • Closest to Mars (how close does Earth get to Mars itself?). The four Mars conditions are shown with their values from NASA’s Mars Fact Sheet. The map colours the most Mars-like land; the list shows the 10 most Mars-like regions, with their score out of 100. Opening one shows each condition for that region next to Mars’s value, and the share of Earth’s land it beats. Below are the agencies’ own analog sites and where they rank, and where the comparison stops, including why the Moon is not ranked here.
  • Earth Analogs (which places are known?). Pick a type of landscape (the 15 Mars landform classes of DoMars16k, or the Moon), then a site on the list or the map. Each site shows why it counts as an analog, the process that shaped it, its climate from NASA POWER, a NASA image, and its published sources.
  • About. The challenge, our solution, how it is built, the NASA and partner agency data with what each is used for, every source, and the team.

How the data is built

Python scripts read the NASA and ESA archives (NASA POWER climate, LRO LOLA, Diviner and Mini-RF, MODIS, ASTER, MOLA, ESA Permafrost_cci) and the GLiM rock map into small data files that ship with the site, so it needs no server and loads fast. The scripts can be rerun from the public repository; rebuilding the Compare data from them gives the same file exactly. The site is checked and deployed by GitHub Actions on every change: formatting, lint, type checks, the 47 tests, and the build. Some results on the home page are worked out from the data at build time, and the build stops if the data ever moves them away from the place named in the text.

How we checked it

  • Two blind results. With no landform data, Discover leads from the Tuktoyaktuk pingos to northern Alaska, inside the area where Jones et al. (2012) mapped 1,247 pingos, and from Death Valley to the coastal desert of southern Peru (Pisco to Acarí), where Hesse (2012) documented dust devil tracks as an analog for dust devil streaks on Mars.
  • Against known analogs. From each of 28 known sites, the closest other known site ranks in the top 0.8% of Earth’s land (random land: 2.5%; climate traits alone: 1.6%; terrain and rock alone: 1.8%).
  • Robustness. With every tolerance changed independently at random by up to ±50%, 40 times, the new regions shown on the site hold in 31 to 38 of 40 runs; we show only regions that hold in at least 30.
  • Closest to Mars, blind. Never given a list of analogs, it ranks Licancabur (NASA High Lakes Project) in the top 0.24% of Earth’s ice-free land, Tso Kar (ISRO’s HOPE analog mission) in the top 0.41% and the Qaidam Basin in the top 0.76%; a random place lands in the top 50%. With the four weights changed at random 40 times, the top region stays on the Tibetan Plateau every time. The known Moon analogs, chosen by rock and landform, rank no better than random land, which is why the Moon is scored in Compare instead.
  • Automated tests. 47 tests guard the scoring, the data and every claim on the Closest to Mars page.

What we found

Earth’s most Mars-like ice-free land is western Tibet, on the Tibetan Plateau (91/100, #1 of 61,443 patches), followed by the high Andes of Bolivia, Argentina and Chile and the Pamirs. And four candidate regions on no analog list we know. Two already match published work: Alaska’s Arctic coastal plain (95%, from Tuktoyaktuk; Jones et al. 2012) and the coastal desert of southern Peru (90%, from Death Valley; Hesse 2012). Two are leads that no paper we found has studied as analogs, and the site labels them that way: Victoria Island in the Canadian Arctic (96%, from Haughton Crater) and Ningxia in northern China (95%, from Green River, Utah).

Limits, stated on the site

No place on Earth matches the Moon’s vacuum, lower gravity, Mars’s thin air or their radiation; the Moon’s polar ice is cold-trapped, not permafrost. Discover compares Earth with Earth: it finds places like a known analog, because no global Mars climate grid exists on the same terms; it matches environment, not landform shape, so it does poorly on impact craters. Closest to Mars ranks how far a place goes toward Mars, not how close it gets, and does not include radiation, ultraviolet light or soil chemistry. Results are regions about 50 km across, to be checked on the ground. Next steps: a landform layer, more Earth sites, and more Mars surface data.

Design and access

The site works on phones and computers, in light and dark mode, with a skip link, keyboard focus and alt text on images. On a phone, explanations open as a sheet that closes with a swipe or the Escape key. It is free and open: no account, no server, and the source code is public.

Tools

Vite, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4, React Router, Leaflet (web app); Python with NumPy, Pillow, rasterio, pyproj and xarray (data scripts); GitHub Pages and GitHub Actions (deployment and checks).

Goals

Give mission planners a sourced shortlist in minutes, help researchers find new candidate regions across the whole planet, and show students how Earth relates to the Moon and Mars, with every number traceable.
